best_for: Long-time Evernote users on Windows or Mac who keep years of clipped pages, scans and notes in it, and who already pay for a plan or are ready to.

points.title: The free plan is a sampler
points.text: Free stops at 50 notes, 1 notebook, 20 tags, 200 attachments and 1 GB of storage, and it syncs to a single device. That is enough to try the app, not to move a real archive into it.

points.title: Starter and Advanced replace the old plans
points.text: Starter raises the caps to 1,000 notes, 20 notebooks, 3 devices and 5 GB. Advanced lifts them to unlimited, with safeguard limits against abuse. The older Personal and Professional plans are retired. Evernote's plan page shows no prices without starting checkout, so check the cost there before you commit.

points.title: Paid plans start with a short trial
points.text: Evernote's FAQ says paid-plan trials usually last 7 days, and you are not charged if you cancel before the trial ends. Set a reminder if you only want a look.

points.title: What it is good at
points.text: The web clipper saves pages, articles and PDFs into your notes, and search reaches text inside images and documents. Scanned receipts and manuals stay findable years later, which is the main reason people stay.

points.title: Account required, no Linux app
points.text: You sign in to an Evernote account to use it. Desktop apps exist for Windows and Mac only; Linux users get the web app in a browser.

points.title: Older Mac versions are not kept here
points.text: The Windows listing keeps 154 versions in x86 and x64 builds, each with a per-user or machine-wide installer. macOS lists only the current universal release, so a Mac downgrade needs another source.
